purpose: Triazolam is used to help people who have trouble falling asleep or staying asleep. It is meant for short-term use only, usually no more than 7 to 10 days. Your doctor may prescribe it if other sleep strategies have not worked well enough.
how_it_works: Triazolam works by calming your brain and nervous system. It boosts the effect of a natural chemical in your brain called GABA, which slows down brain activity and helps you feel relaxed and sleepy. Think of it like turning down the volume on an overactive brain so you can drift off to sleep.
common_side_effects: Drowsiness or feeling groggy the next morning, dizziness, headache, feeling unsteady or clumsy, and memory problems (you may not remember things that happened after taking the pill). Some people feel anxious or have unusual dreams.
warnings: This medicine can be habit-forming, so only take it exactly as prescribed and do not take it longer than directed. Never mix it with alcohol, opioid pain medicines, or other sleep aids — this can be very dangerous and even life-threatening. Some people have done things like sleepwalking, sleep-driving, or eating while not fully awake. Tell your doctor right away if this happens. Do not take it during pregnancy. Do not suddenly stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 0.125 mg to 0.25 mg taken by mouth right before bedtime. Older adults are usually started on the lowest dose (0.125 mg) to reduce the risk of falls and confusion. Always take it only when you have a full 7 to 8 hours available for sleep.
